title: Git & Version Control
subtitle: Weeks 3-4: track every change with confidence
description: Version control from first principles: the working tree and staging area, commits and history, branching and merging, remotes and pull requests, safely rewriting history, and recovering from mistakes.

lessons.title: What Version Control Is
lessons.body:
Version control is a system that records the history of a project so you can see what changed, when, and why. Git stores your project inside a **repository** (the `.git` folder), a database of **snapshots**. Each snapshot is a **commit**: a complete record of the tracked files at that moment, plus the author, timestamp, message, and a pointer to its parent commit. Because every commit points at its parent, the commits form a chain — the project's history.

Three areas describe where a change lives:

- The **working tree** is the folder you edit.
- The **staging area** (or index) is a holding pen for changes you want in the next snapshot.
- The **repository** is the committed history.

`HEAD` is a special pointer to the commit you currently have checked out — usually the tip of your current branch. As you commit, `HEAD` moves forward.

The **WHY** matters: people without version control keep `report_final_v3_FINAL_really.doc` copies. Copies cannot tell you *why* a line changed, cannot merge two people's work, and cannot be rolled back cleanly. Git records snapshots cheaply (it stores each file's content once and reuses it) and lets you compare, branch, and undo with confidence.

exercises.prompt: Where do changes live once you have marked them for the next commit but not yet committed?
exercises.hint: It sits between your working tree and a commit.
exercises.explain: You stage changes with git add; they wait in the staging area until git commit writes them into history.

exercises.prompt: What does HEAD point to in a normal repository?
options: The commit currently checked out, usually the tip of your branch
The oldest commit in the project
exercises.hint: It is where you are right now, and it moves when you commit.
exercises.explain: HEAD is a pointer to the current commit, normally the tip of the active branch; committing advances it.

exercises.prompt: Write the exact command that shows a compact, one-line-per-commit history
exercises.hint: git log with a single flag that shortens each entry.
exercises.explain: git log --oneline prints the short hash and subject of each commit.

exercises.prompt: Put the journey of a single change into the correct order
items: Edit the file in the working tree
Stage it with git add
Create the snapshot with git commit
The change becomes part of the committed history
exercises.explain: Working tree, then staging area, then commit — this is the loop you will repeat hundreds of times.
exercises.hint: A change is edited, then staged, then committed.

lessons.title: Your First Repository
lessons.body:
Create a repository with `git init`, which makes a hidden `.git` folder in the current directory. That folder *is* the repository; delete it and Git stops tracking the project. You do not need a remote server to start.

The day-to-day loop:

```
git init                 # start a repository here
git status               # what changed, what is staged
git add README.md        # stage one file
git add .                # stage everything changed
git commit -m "Add README with setup steps"
git log --oneline        # compact history
git diff                 # unstaged changes
git diff --staged        # exactly what you are about to commit
```

Check `git diff --staged` before every commit. It is the last chance to catch a stray debug line or a password.

Use a `.gitignore` file to list paths Git should never track — `node_modules/`, `.env`, `*.log`. Anything already tracked stays tracked, so add secrets to `.gitignore` *before* the first commit.

A good **commit message** has a short imperative subject ("Fix login timeout", not "fixed stuff") of about 50 characters, then a blank line, then a body explaining **why** the change was needed. Future-you, reading `git log` at 2am, is the audience.

exercises.prompt: What does git init actually do?
options: Creates a hidden .git folder, turning the current directory into a repository
exercises.hint: It only sets up local bookkeeping; no commit and no server involved.
exercises.explain: git init just creates the .git directory; you still need to stage and commit your files.

exercises.prompt: Write the exact command that stages every changed and new file in the current directory
exercises.hint: git add, then the symbol meaning everything here.
exercises.explain: git add . (or -A / --all) stages all changes so the next commit includes them.

exercises.prompt: Write a good commit message for a change that adds a `.gitignore` and stops tracking `node_modules`. It needs a short imperative subject line, a blank line, then a body explaining why.

patterns.m: a short subject line, then a blank line before the body
mention what is being ignored (node_modules, .env or .gitignore)
a body paragraph of at least a sentence explaining why

exercises.solution:
Stop tracking node_modules and local env files

Committing node_modules bloats the repository and creates constant, meaningless merge conflicts. Add .gitignore entries so build output, dependencies and local environment files stay out of version control.
exercises.explain: A tight subject, a blank line, then a body that explains the reason — exactly what a reviewer needs.
exercises.hint: Subject under ~50 characters, blank line, then why.

exercises.prompt: Put the daily commit loop in the correct order
items: Edit your files
Stage the changes with git add
Review with git diff --staged
Commit with a clear message
exercises.explain: Review before you commit; it is your last guard against secrets and debug code.
exercises.hint: Edit, stage, review, then commit.

lessons.title: Branching and Merging
lessons.body:
A **branch** is just a movable pointer to a commit. `main` is the default one. Creating a branch costs almost nothing — it writes a name pointing at the current commit. This is why Git encourages a branch for every feature or fix.

```
git branch feature/login     # create a branch at the current commit
git switch feature/login     # move onto it (older syntax: git checkout)
git switch -c fix/typo       # create and switch in one step
git switch main              # back to main
git merge feature/login      # bring its commits into main
git branch -d feature/login  # delete it once merged
```

When you merge, Git finds the **merge base** — the last commit the two branches shared. If `main` has not moved since you branched, Git simply slides the pointer forward: a **fast-forward**, and no new commit appears. If both branches have new commits, Git creates a **merge commit** with two parents, joining the histories.

Conflicts happen when both branches changed the same lines. Git marks the file with `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>` and pauses the merge. Edit the file to the version you want, delete the markers, then:

```
git add app.js
git merge --continue
# or back out entirely with:
git merge --abort
```

exercises.prompt: In Git, what is a branch?
options: A movable pointer to a commit
A full copy of the project folder
A remote server holding your code
exercises.hint: Creating one is nearly free — it is only a name pointing somewhere.
exercises.explain: A branch is a lightweight pointer to a commit; that is why branching is cheap and encouraged.

exercises.prompt: Write the single command that creates and switches to a new branch named feature/login
exercises.hint: switch with the create flag -c, or checkout with -b.
exercises.explain: git switch -c feature/login creates the branch and moves you onto it in one step.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps for resolving a merge conflict in the correct order
items: Open the conflicted file and find the <<<<<<< markers
Edit the file to the version you want and delete the markers
Stage the resolved file with git add
Finish the merge with git merge --continue
exercises.explain: Resolve, clean up the markers, stage, then continue — or use git merge --abort to start over.
exercises.hint: Fix the file first, then stage, then continue.

exercises.prompt: When does Git create a merge commit instead of doing a fast-forward?
options: When both branches have new commits since they diverged
Only when there is a conflict
Whenever the branch name contains a slash
exercises.hint: It needs two lines of history to join.
exercises.explain: If both branches advanced, Git joins the two histories with a merge commit that has two parents.

lessons.title: Remotes and Collaboration
lessons.body:
A **remote** is a named URL to another copy of the repository, usually on GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket. `origin` is the default name for the one you cloned from.

```
git clone git@github.com:acme/app.git   # copy a remote repo locally
git remote -v                            # list remotes and their URLs
git fetch origin                         # download new commits, change nothing
git pull                                 # fetch, then merge into the current branch
git push -u origin feature/login        # upload; -u links branch to its upstream
git push                                 # later pushes just work
```

The key distinction: `fetch` only downloads — your files stay put, and you decide what to merge. `pull` is `fetch` plus `merge` (or `rebase`). Support engineers prefer to `fetch` first because it is safe and lets you inspect incoming work with `git log origin/main`.

The **fork / branch / pull request** workflow is how most teams collaborate. You rarely push to `main` directly. Instead you create a short-lived branch, push it, and open a **pull request** (PR). Reviewers comment, CI runs tests, and only then is it merged. A **fork** is a server-side copy under your own account, used when you lack write access to the original.

Good collaborators fetch often, keep branches small, and write PR descriptions that explain the *what* and the *why*.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?
options: fetch downloads only; pull downloads and merges into your branch
fetch deletes local changes; pull keeps them
exercises.hint: One of them changes your working files, the other does not.
exercises.explain: fetch is safe and read-only; pull is fetch followed by a merge (or rebase) into the current branch.

exercises.prompt: Write the command to push your local branch feature/login to origin for the first time, linking it to its upstream
exercises.hint: push with the upstream flag -u, the remote name, then the branch.
exercises.explain: The -u flag sets the upstream so future git push and git pull need no arguments.

exercises.prompt: Put the fork / branch / pull request workflow in the correct order
items: Create a branch (or fork the repository)
Push the branch to your remote
Open a pull request describing the change
Review, run CI, and merge
exercises.explain: Work happens on a branch; only reviewed and tested code reaches main.
exercises.hint: You never push straight to main.

exercises.prompt: What does git clone do?
options: Copies a remote repository, including its history, to your machine
Uploads your local commits to a server
exercises.hint: It is the first command you run on a project you have not worked on before.
exercises.explain: git clone downloads the full repository and checks out the default branch, setting origin as the remote.

lessons.title: Rewriting History Safely
lessons.body:
History is editable until you share it. **Never rewrite commits that others have already pulled** — their copies will diverge and cause pain. That single rule governs everything here.

`git revert` is the safe undo: it creates a *new* commit that reverses an earlier one. It keeps history intact, so it is the right tool on a shared branch.

```
git revert a1b2c3d            # new commit that undoes that one
git rebase main               # replay your branch's commits on top of main
git rebase -i HEAD~3          # edit the last three commits
git cherry-pick a1b2c3d       # copy one commit onto the current branch
git reset --soft HEAD~1       # undo the commit, keep changes staged
git reset --mixed HEAD~1      # undo the commit, keep changes unstaged (default)
git reset --hard HEAD~1       # undo the commit AND discard the changes
```

An **interactive rebase** (`-i`) opens a list of actions: `pick`, `reword` (edit the message), `squash` (fold into the previous commit) and `drop`. It is how you turn five messy "wip" commits into one clean one before opening a PR.

The three `reset` modes differ only in what they do with your changes: `--soft` keeps them staged, `--mixed` keeps them in the working tree, and `--hard` destroys them. `--hard` is the dangerous one — check `git status` first and commit or stash anything you are unsure about.

exercises.prompt: You pushed a commit to a shared branch and need to undo it. Which command is safest?
exercises.hint: It adds a new commit instead of removing an old one.
exercises.explain: revert creates a new commit that reverses the change, so everyone's history stays consistent.

exercises.prompt: Which git reset mode discards your uncommitted changes completely?
exercises.hint: The strictest of the three; it wipes the working tree.
exercises.explain: --hard resets the working tree and index, so uncommitted changes are lost. Use with care.

exercises.prompt: Write the command that copies the single commit a1b2c3d onto your current branch
exercises.hint: It is named after picking a cherry off another branch.
exercises.explain: git cherry-pick applies just that commit's changes onto the current branch.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of squashing the last three commits with an interactive rebase in order
items: Run git rebase -i HEAD~3
Change the later picks to squash in the editor
Write the combined commit message
Save and close; Git rewrites the history
exercises.explain: Interactive rebase opens a list; marking commits squash folds them into the previous one.
exercises.hint: Start the rebase, edit the list, then edit the message.

lessons.title: Recovering from Mistakes
lessons.body:
Git rarely loses work. Even after a bad `reset --hard`, the old commits still exist in the **reflog**, a local log of where `HEAD` has been.

```
git reflog                     # recent HEAD positions
git reset --hard HEAD@{1}      # jump back to where you were
git restore app.js             # discard working-tree changes to a file
git restore --staged app.js    # unstage a file, keep the edit
git commit --amend -m "Better subject"   # fix the last commit (message or files)
git stash                      # park uncommitted changes
git stash pop                  # bring them back
git tag v1.2.0                 # lightweight tag on the current commit
git tag -a v1.2.0 -m "Release 1.2.0"     # annotated tag
git push origin v1.2.0         # tags are not pushed automatically
```

To undo a commit you already pushed, use `git revert` (Lesson 5): it is honest and safe. To undo a local commit you have not pushed, `git reset` is fine.

`git stash` is a scratchpad for "I need to switch branches but my work is half-done": it saves the working tree and index, then clears them. `git stash pop` reapplies and removes the entry.

**Tags** mark specific commits, usually releases. Annotated tags carry a message and date and are what `git describe` uses. Because tags are not pushed by default, always `git push --tags` or push them by name when you cut a release.

exercises.prompt: What does the git reflog record?
options: Where HEAD and branch tips have recently pointed locally
The list of remote pull requests
exercises.hint: It is your safety net after a reset or a bad rebase.
exercises.explain: The reflog is a local history of reference movements, so you can recover commits that seem lost.

exercises.prompt: Write the command that lists recent HEAD positions so you can recover a lost commit
exercises.hint: Short for reference log.
exercises.explain: git reflog shows recent HEAD movements; reset to an entry like HEAD@{1} to recover.

exercises.prompt: You have half-finished work but need to switch branches urgently. What is the tidy option?
exercises.hint: It parks your changes so you can retrieve them later.
exercises.explain: git stash saves the working tree and index away, letting you switch branches cleanly; git stash pop restores.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of using the stash in the correct order
items: Make your edits on the current branch
Run git stash to park them
Switch to the other branch and do the urgent work
Run git stash pop to bring your edits back
exercises.explain: Stash, switch, work, then pop — a clean way to context-switch without committing half a change.
exercises.hint: Park, switch, then restore.
